Circles and a Limit

LimitsAlgebra
Game: This is a picture to explore, not a game with a winner; two circles meet and a line through their meeting point runs out to a spot called E.
How to play: Drag the top of the small circle, or slide the control, to change its size and watch E. Tick "hint" for helper lines and "names" to label the points.

Drag the bright handle on top of the small circle, or focus the picture and use the arrow keys. Enter toggles the hint.

2.00 E at x = 11.66
Look for the math

Two circles, one shrinking, and a line that keeps meeting the axis somewhere new. You might expect that point to run away as the little circle disappears. It does not: it settles down at a definite spot. That spot is the whole puzzle.

Set up the picture

The fixed circle has radius 3 and sits at (3, 0), so it passes through the origin O. The small circle is centred at O with radius r. It touches the positive y-axis at A = (0, r) and meets the fixed circle in the upper half-plane at B. Stretch the line through A and B until it crosses the x-axis: that crossing is E.

Find where E lands

The two circles cross where x = r²/(2a) and y = r·√(1 − (r/(2a))²), taking a = 3 for the fixed circle. Putting that point B together with A = (0, r) and solving for where the line reaches y = 0 gives

x_E = 2a·(1 + √(1 − (r/(2a))²))

As r gets tiny, the square root goes to 1, so x_E goes to 2a·2 = 4a. For a = 3 that is 12: the point E has a limit at (12, 0). The logic test checked the formula and the crossing point for hundreds of radii on fixed circles of many sizes, and every value agreed.

Four times as far

The article says the limit sits "four times farther from the origin than the centre of the fixed circle." The centre is a from the origin, and the limit is 4a from it, so the claim is exactly right: 4 × 3 = 12. The test confirmed limit = 4a for a = 1, 2, 3, 5, 10. The applet even hard-codes the same answer: when the line through A and B becomes too flat to cross the axis, it places E at O.x + 4 × (fixed radius) — the very spot the formula approaches.

The geometric proof

Tick "hint" to see why no algebra is needed. Three choices show three proofs: they add helper points D and F and dashed lines that turn the picture into right angles and midpoints, from which the ratio 4 : 1 can be read off. One tiny quirk of the original: in the third proof it relabels the right-hand point as C, moving the name off the bottom of the small circle; this port keeps that quirk. Everything else is the puzzle the article states.

Try sliding the radius down to its smallest value: does E ever pass 12, or only get closer and closer?
